children: By Joy Wiltermuth and Christine Idzelis
Other stocks are in a bear market, which could be bad timing with the crucial holiday shopping period ahead
The stock market is heading into a short holiday week for Thanksgiving on fragile footing. That could be a bad sign for the economy.
At least grocery stores still give away "free" turkeys.
Investors might want to do a multiyear recounting of their blessings this Thanksgiving, given the stock market's huge gains since 2022, but also the recent lurch lower.

The Nasdaq Composite COMP wiped out its yearly gain in Friday's market carnage - plus some. What was left over from the S&P 500 SPX and Dow Jones Industrial Average's DJIA earlier charge higher in 2026 was hanging on by a thread.

"This is becoming one of the worst losing streaks we've ever seen," said Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at the Carson Group, pointing to the S&P 500's seven-day skid as the longest since February 2020.

A mixed bag of woes were coming home to roost all at once - with only six weeks until year's end. Nagging questions about the potential impact to the artificial-intelligence boom from November's "blue tsunami" in midterm elections have been growing louder as Democrats get closer to taking control of Congress in January.

The fallout from Jensen Huang's shocking resignation as Nvidia's (NVDA) CEO has been intensifying, with shares of the AI chipmaker now down more than 32% in 2026. Federal Reserve officials also have been talking louder lately about the potential need for a speedier pace of rate hikes.
All that has "caused a perfect storm for investors as we head into Thanksgiving week," Detrick told MarketWatch.

All three indexes were in a correction of at least 10% from their previous record highs. The S&P 500 was up only 0.9% on the year through Friday, the Dow was 0.2% higher and the Nasdaq was down 2.7%, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
A fear is that significant losses in the stock market could cause wealthier families to pull back. Their spending and the AI boom have been keeping the economy humming.
Related: Chip stocks see $2.3 trillion weekly wipeout as panic grips the AI trade
The recent painful pullback comes at a precarious time, since it's right before the critical holiday shopping season for retailers.
Game-changing November
Over a little more than a week, investors have witnessed a stunning drop in the stocks at the core of the four-year bull market.
Right before Veterans Day on Nov. 11, the S&P 500 was up more than 10% for the year, heading for a bigger-than-average annualized gain, as MarketWatch reported.
"The market is in a pretty fragile state right now," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial. "The sentiment is clearly negative."
The good news is that the U.S. economy appears to be gathering steam, even though the market has increasingly fixated on multiple signs that a recession could be drawing closer.
Heading into the holiday-shortened week, "technicals will become more important in terms of gauging near-term support" for the stock market, Saglimbene added.
Yet for long-term investors, it's helpful to remember that since its bear-market closing low of 3,577 in October 2022, the S&P 500 has gained 93.2%, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

That might be good to keep in mind in the coming days. Thanksgiving week traditionally can be "quite volatile," as trading volume is usually low with a lot of people are taking off for the holiday, said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide.

"You have an easier time creating disruptive markets," Hackett added. Also, with the stock market's truncated session on Black Friday, investors may "overreact to initial indications" about holiday spending, potentially injecting some market volatility, he said.
The U.S. stock market will close early on Black Friday, at 1 p.m. Eastern.

Kevin Gordon, head of macro research and strategy at Charles Schwab, noted that the S&P 500's information-technology sector XX:SP500.45 already had fallen into a bear market, defined as a drop of at least 20% from a previous closing record.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was down 18.1% at Friday's close from its October record close, near a bear market, with the "AI creator group" generally under significant pressure, Gordon said.
"You can have non-recessionary corrections" and bear markets, Gordon added.
